title: Data Transfer Rate Converter: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Data Transfer Rate Converter: Convert bits and bytes per second and estimate download time for a chosen file size. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it,…
content:
The [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Convert bits and bytes per second and estimate download time for a chosen file size. Enter your transfer rate, rate unit and file size for time estimate and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Network speeds are usually advertised in bits per second, while file sizes and transfer monitors often use bytes per second. One byte contains eight bits, so 100 megabits per second corresponds to 12.5 megabytes per second before overhead. This converter covers decimal bit and byte units and adds an ideal download-time estimate for a decimal-gigabyte file. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Data Transfer Rate Converter

Start by entering your transfer rate, then choosing your rate unit from the list and finally entering your file size for time estimate (GB). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the speed and choose bits or bytes carefully; capital B denotes bytes.
2. Add a file size in decimal GB to see the theoretical transfer time at the full entered rate.
3. Allow extra time for protocol overhead, server limits, Wi-Fi conditions, congestion and other traffic.

## Formula

Bytes per second = bits per second ÷ 8. Ideal seconds = file size in GB × 8,000,000,000 ÷ rate in bits per second.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. At 100 Mbit/s, the byte rate is 12.5 MB/s. A 1 GB file takes 80 seconds in the ideal decimal model, before network and protocol overhead. Try the same figures in the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Transfer rate: 100, Rate unit: Megabits per second, File size for time estimate: 1 GB), the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) returns Megabits per second: 100 Mbit/s, Megabytes per second: 12.5 MB/s, Gigabits per second: 0.1 Gbit/s, Gigabytes per second: 0.0125 GB/s, Ideal time for 1 GB: 80 seconds (1.33 minutes). The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Temperature Converter](/temperature-converter) is worth a look before you finish.

## Megabits and megabytes are different

The abbreviation Mb means megabits and MB means megabytes, an eightfold difference at the same decimal prefix. Internet service is commonly sold in Mbit/s, while operating systems may display downloads in MB/s or MiB/s. This page uses decimal units consistently: 1 GB = 8,000,000,000 bits and 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.

## Why real downloads take longer

The time estimate assumes the entire capacity is continuously available to one transfer. Packet headers, retransmissions, encryption, server throughput, storage speed and network contention reduce useful throughput. It also uses decimal GB, not GiB; one GiB is about 7.37% larger than one GB.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Check capitalisation: bit/s and B/s are not interchangeable.
- Use a sustained transfer rate rather than a momentary speed-test peak for planning.
- For GiB files, multiply the decimal-GB estimate by 1.073741824.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is 100 Mbps the same as 100 MB/s?

No. 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s because there are eight bits in a byte. Capitalisation and the /s unit are essential. Try it with your own numbers in the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does this use binary or decimal units?

Decimal. kbit, Mbit, kB and MB use powers of 1,000. Binary MiB and GiB are different units and are not used in the displayed estimate. Try it with your own numbers in the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why is my actual speed lower?

The result is theoretical. Server limits, Wi-Fi quality, congestion, protocol overhead and device performance can all reduce real throughput. Try it with your own numbers in the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Data Transfer Rate Converter use?

Bytes per second = bits per second ÷ 8. Ideal seconds = file size in GB × 8,000,000,000 ÷ rate in bits per second. You can see it in action in the [Data Transfer Rate Converter](/data-transfer-rate-converter) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
